j.learned_fact: Library books have a due-date stamp and must be returned so other children can read them.
j.thinking_skill: accepts a simple reason for a rule (sharing)
j.notes: Two lessons (due dates and "words tell the story") are bolted together and delivered by the mother as explanation; Amelia's sudden question about print is implausible for a child who already wanted a book, and she does the reading herself at the end.

j.learned_fact: Heat from the stove makes the pot hot, so you stand back; blowing on hot soup cools it before tasting.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (heat makes pot hot, so stand back)
j.notes: Scarlett's line "The fire makes the pot hot. So I stand back" is too neatly explanatory for a 4-year-old and reads as a bolted-on safety lesson; the opening "was tired" never connects to anything, and the orange-rolling is filler.

j.learned_fact: The five senses pair with body parts: eyes see, nose smells, fingers touch, tongue tastes, ears hear.
j.thinking_skill: identifies a problem and asks for help to solve it
j.notes: The senses checklist is visible: "with her eyes/nose/fingers/tongue/ears" is repetitive and stilted, and the hearing line is awkwardly reported in past tense as dialogue. Plot is minimal but age-appropriate.

j.learned_fact: Mixing red and yellow paint makes orange — true.
j.thinking_skill: combines two known things to predict/achieve a new result
j.notes: Color naming feels slightly bolted on, and details like "painted a red stem" and "made a big noise" are odd; also a bit long and dense for a 3-year-old's listening span, with no repetition or rhythm.

j.learned_fact: Hot water can hurt your hands, and cool water soothes a burn. But the tap detail is misleading: by plumbing convention the left tap is hot and the right is cold, the reverse of the story.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect and repeats the action that worked
j.notes: The tap-handle logic is reversed from real life, so the one concrete fact a child could carry away is wrong; "rough little hands" is an odd word choice, and a mild burn is slightly scary framing for age 3.

j.learned_fact: A zipper only works if you push the two bottom sides together into the slider first, then pull up.
j.thinking_skill: notices a cause (parts not joined at the bottom) and fixes it
j.notes: Sequence slips: the coat is zipped before "one arm in, two arms in," and the "loud sheep" bit is an unexplained non sequitur. "It went up all by itself" slightly undercuts the fact that Nora did it.

j.learned_fact: Pressing save keeps a drawing inside the tablet so it is still there later; the power button makes the screen sleep.
j.thinking_skill: asks where the drawing went and checks the screen to confirm
j.notes: The saving moment is told rather than shown ("He had pressed save" is stated after the fact, never depicted), so the key idea is asserted rather than discovered; stakes are very low.

j.learned_fact: A long tool (a spoon) can reach a ball stuck under furniture; taking turns means first one person, then the other.
j.thinking_skill: reuses a solution seen once (tool to reach under furniture)
j.notes: The rain/window detail is unconnected filler, and the opening "roll it down the stairs" idea is dropped without resolution; flat, listy sentences with no real feeling or ending.

j.learned_fact: If you want something someone else has, you can wait (counting to ten) instead of grabbing; a loud bang can turn out to be an ordinary thing like a door closing.
j.thinking_skill: recognizes her own feeling and delays acting on it
j.notes: Reads like three social-emotional checkboxes (helping, patience, loud noise) strung together rather than one story; the line "Bunnies hop wild in the yard at the store by our house" is garbled and confusing for a 3-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Glue holds a paper shape in place so it stops slipping; yesterday/today/tomorrow name past, present and future days.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (glue stops slipping)
j.notes: The time-word scaffolding (yesterday/today/tomorrow, "His problem was that...") feels bolted on, and the muddled sentence "today the sun is dry and flat" confuses the real sun with the paper one — too abstract and unclear for a three-year-old.

j.learned_fact: Tipping a cup slightly when pouring keeps milk from spilling; a thicker dab of butter stays on toast instead of sliding off. The butter explanation is shaky — butter slides because it is cold/hard or the toast hot, not because it was "too thin."
j.thinking_skill: notices a problem and adjusts one variable (amount of butter) to fix it
j.notes: The central "why" is explained with a semi-false physics claim, and the petal simile is an adult flourish in a child's mouth; otherwise warm, well-paced and age-appropriate. A 4-year-old using a knife alone goes unremarked.

j.learned_fact: Blown-out candles make smoke — "The fire made the smoke."
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect
j.notes: Warm and sensory, but sentence length, similes ("like a little gray snake") and vocabulary ("bobbed", "struck a match", "curled") sit above a 3-year-old; the causal insight is stated rather than discovered, and the takeaway is thin.

j.learned_fact: A grill gives off heat you can feel from nearby, and hot things can hurt you — so stay back.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (warm air means hot, so step back)
j.notes: Reads like a safety-checklist (stool, stay close, hot grill, sun hat) rather than one story; the sun hat detail appears from nowhere and the apple and grill episodes barely connect.

j.learned_fact: Counting to six; adding one more to five makes six.
j.thinking_skill: recounts to check a total and adds one to fix the shortfall
j.notes: The line "The bag has five because I stopped at five" is oddly metacognitive for a 4-year-old character and slightly stilted; the "bag felt too light" cue is a weak way to notice a miscount.

j.learned_fact: Many people clapping together sounds louder than one person clapping alone; also counting to three.
j.thinking_skill: notices one cause and effect (more clappers = louder)
j.notes: The repeated "one clap, two claps, three claps" feels like a drilled device rather than play, and Lydia's tidy explanation line sounds adult for a three-year-old. Mommy and Grandma appear out of nowhere mid-scene.

j.learned_fact: A conflict over one toy can be solved by offering an alternative both people are happy with (sharing/trading); colour words red and green.
j.thinking_skill: finds an alternative that satisfies both parties
j.notes: Simple, warm and age-appropriate, but the "deep in the cart with the bread" and "present for my birthday" details are confusing/unmotivated, and the resolution is a bit too easy for real conflict learning.

j.learned_fact: The five senses and their body parts: eyes see, ears hear, nose smells, tongue tastes, skin feels — accurate.
j.thinking_skill: recalls and applies a memorized list to a real object
j.notes: The whole story is a quiz drill rather than a plot; Mommy's "Almost. Say it right." correction is puzzling, and "She stopped cutting the apple" contradicts the earlier image of her simply holding it.

j.learned_fact: Kicking harder pushes against the water and moves you forward.
j.thinking_skill: tries again with more force and notices the cause and effect
j.notes: Andrew's line "The water is easy to push" sounds like an adult-inserted physics explanation, not a 3-year-old; the sudden "time for a nap" ending is abrupt and unearned.

j.learned_fact: Cold hard butter spreads better after you push it slowly and it warms and softens; pouring slowly keeps milk from spilling.
j.thinking_skill: adjusts her method after a failure (notices cause and effect)
j.notes: Charming and age-appropriate; "stormy-day" appears from nowhere since no weather was established, and the ending's refusal to share is a slightly odd note.

j.learned_fact: A shot feels like a quick pinch and is over fast; counting to three can help you get through it. The nurse's claim the needle is tiny "because it only needs a little bit" is a vague, half-true explanation.
j.thinking_skill: asks a why-question and links needle size to amount of medicine
j.notes: The line "She gave him a weak arm right after, then flexed it strong" is garbled and will confuse a 4-year-old, as will "drew a small line on her skin." Otherwise sentences are short and age-appropriate, but the takeaway is thin.
